title: Caritas
hookLine: the Church's charity agencies carry the word caritas, love, to the ends of the earth

lines: A FLOOD, A TRUCK, A BLANKET.
A KEY FOR A NEW FAMILY.
cards: A flood comes through a town, and a few days later a truck pulls up with water, blankets and people in vests. A refugee family lands in a strange city, and someone meets them with a key to an apartment.

A man leaves prison with nowhere to go, and a desk somewhere has his name on a list. Look at the logo on the vest or the door, and often enough it says Caritas, or Catholic Charities, or Catholic Relief Services.
One Latin word sits behind all of them.

teach.b: You met this word back on day two hundred ninety-six: God is charity. Caritas is the Latin the Church uses for love, the self-giving kind, and older English Bibles render it charity.
Paul describes it to the Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Charity is patient, is kind." So charity, first, isn't a donation. It's a way of loving.

Then a decision in Acts. The first Christians in Jerusalem share food with widows every day, and a complaint goes up: some widows are being missed. The apostles don't shrug, and they don't drop everything else.
They choose seven men to take charge of the daily serving, so no one is skipped.
Pope Benedict the Sixteenth, in his letter God is Love, points to that moment: from then on, serving the poor is organized, and it's part of who the Church is. Then his big claim.

The Church can't do without three things: proclaiming the word, celebrating the sacraments, and the service of charity. Take one away and something essential is missing. Charity isn't an extra for spare time.

And what that grew into: some parishes run food pantries, dioceses run charities, and Catholic agencies work across borders, joined in a confederation called Caritas Internationalis. Benedict adds one warning.
The people who serve need hearts formed by love, not just training, so that a person in need meets a person, not a process.
A blanket handed over coldly is still a blanket. Handed over with love, it's caritas.

how: Catholics give to charity through parish collections, diocesan appeals and agencies such as Caritas, Catholic Charities and Catholic Relief Services, and some parishes run food pantries and volunteer programs of their own.

o: Latin for a gift of money to the poor
Latin for the Church's welfare office
Latin for love that gives itself away

p: chosen to serve the daily tables
three things the Church can't do without

s: in the old Bibles, charity is love itself: charity is patient, is kind.
Benedict XVI called charity an optional extra for the Church
he named it with the word and the sacraments as part of who the Church is.
in Acts, the apostles chose seven men to serve the widows' tables
a complaint went up that some widows were missed, and seven were chosen for the daily serving.

games.q: you're an apostle in Jerusalem. some widows are being missed at the daily serving, and you're already stretched thin. what do you do?
o: stop preaching and serve the tables yourselves.
choose seven people to take charge of the serving.
games.why: they choose seven men for the work, so no one is skipped and the preaching goes on. Benedict XVI points to this as charity becoming organized.

practice: If you're able, choose one group that serves people in need, near or far, and give it something, money, an hour, a bag of clothes, any size at all.
Then bring to mind one person it might reach, someone you'll never meet, and hold them for a few breaths. If you pray, offer the gift and the person to God.

wordCard.voice: Caritas. Latin for the love that gives itself. This week's road: social friendship, four verbs, people before machines, no one for sale, meant for all, active nonviolence, and now charity everywhere.

orig.note: Latin: love, the self-giving kind, rendered charity in older English Bibles.

carryVoice: Your line: charity everywhere. A name on a van or a door, and a love underneath it. Rest well.
